item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm sorry, I prefer my top-secret world-spanning organizations to actually face realistic consequences for being so.

Look, the Foundation literally cannot be larger than a million people, okay? Even with all the amnesiacs in the world, that won't be enough to stop a catastrophic secrecy breach in only a few years. A tiny, tiny fraction of that is medical research. Because, get this, the Foundation has no actual reason to do medical research. SCPs are either so different from normal stuff that any research conclusions drawn have no relevance anywhere else, or respond to standard stuff in which case the Foundation won't need to do much of anything.

The ruthlessness argument is valid to a point, but that won't get it far enough. Plus, the Foundation focuses pretty heavily on SCPs. They aren't every industry ever, and they certainly aren't better at every industry ever than every industry ever.

Anyhow, this is getting me far angrier than I ought to let it. Of course I have strong opinions. What's the point of having opinions otherwise? Night all.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Yet, even without the paraphernalia attached to either a government-oversight medical research area, or a university with a School of Medicine / Hospital attached, a lot of reasonably modern medical knowledge has been built on results of what is usually described as medical torture, perpetrated by individuals such as Mengele & Wirths (Nazi regime), and Unit 731 of the Imperial Japanese Army.

Arguably, some of the testing logs use D-Class in a similar vein. A claim that the Foundation is at the "forefront of medical research" would essentially only be marketing spin, given that the Foundation deals entirely with objects/entities/effects that are outside of the normal course of human experience.

It isn't a bad 'orientation' style article. The last line about the top-hat guy seems a bit irrelevant though.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: Gah! The Foundation is not remotely at the forefront of medical research. Dealing with dangerous stuff doesn't really mean much of anything in that regard. The Foundation cannot have a very large or well-connected medical research division, due to secrecy and scale reasons. They are smaller than, say, Hopkins or NIH, have less medical resources than Hopkins or NIH, and probably have worse scientists than any major research institution out there. The Foundation is very good at some things, but not every last little thing. And there's no way that it makes sense for them to be anything but crap at medical research.
